text: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions LogSync chips, measuring approximately 4x2 mm. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 - CC-BY-SA 4.0 EPFL researchers have developed an implantable neural chip that

record.title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions
record.author: giuliomagnifico
record.article_text: LogSync chips, measuring approximately 4x2 mm. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 - CC-BY-SA 4.0 EPFL researchers have developed an implantable neural chip that tracks communication across brain regions, identifying cognitive and emotional states in real time. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic technique that delivers electrical pulses to specific areas of the brain via an implant to modulate neural activity. It is already widely used for movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, and researchers are increasingly exploring its potential for severe psychiatric illnesses including major depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. However, most existing DBS systems operate in what engineers call an “open loop” manner: stimulation is delivered according to predefined settings rather than continuously adapting to the patient’s brain activity. Even among closed-loop, or adaptive systems, many rely on signals recorded from a single brain region. This is a major limitation for psychiatric disorders, where clinically relevant information may be distributed across networks of interacting brain regions. “Our work is based on the growing body of research suggesting that psychiatric disorders arise more from disruptions in communication between brain regions than from dysfunction of any single region,” explains Mahsa Shoaran, head of the Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab in EPFL’s School of Engineering and Neuro-X Institute. Shoaran and her team have developed a low-power, implantable neural system-on-chip. Dubbed LogSync, it records brain activity and extracts biomarkers that describe the strength of brain waves (oscillations) and synchrony between signals from different brain regions. A machine-learning algorithm then analyzes these network-level biomarkers to distinguish cognitive and emotional states, and generate stimulation triggers when specific states are detected. The work, published in the IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits , was developed as part of a CHF 6.6 million grant from the US National Institute for Mental health (NIMH) to develop implantable systems capable of measuring and controlling oscillatory brain networks for severe psychiatric illnesses, particularly mood and anxiety disorders. It builds on the lab's previous work on brain-to-text decoding and closed-loop neuromodulation , extending these concepts to network-level biomarkers and adaptive decoding for future psychiatric therapies. The researchers evaluated LogSync using human brain recordings from previous psychiatric experiments. One dataset captured changes in cognitive engagement while performing a mental task, while another captured emotional arousal as participants viewed video clips. The algorithm distinguished these cognitive and emotional states from the neural recordings alone. In further experiments conducted in rats at the University of Minnesota, the implant tracked ongoing oscillations and generated stimulation triggers at predefined phases of brain activity. Shoaran says that major challenge was achieving all this functionality while working within the very limited power budget of an implantable system. “Our entire system is co-designed, meaning the algorithms and hardware are developed together with the constraints of implant in mind. This approach helped us achieve network-level neural signal processing and decoding on a single chip, while keeping power consumption under 200 microwatts — a fraction of that typically required by many implantable neural-interface systems,” she says. Another innovation is LogSync’s use of logarithmic computations, which simplify the complex operations needed for brain-network analysis and real-time biomarker extraction and decoding. LogSync's initial validation focused on psychiatric applications. But the capability to extract brain-network biomarkers to trigger precisely timed stimulation is broadly applicable across next-generation neurotechnology, including adaptive DBS for movement disorders, closed-loop non-invasive stimulation, and emerging focused-ultrasound interfaces. In parallel, the laboratory is developing new machine-learning methods that learn directly from neural recordings rather than predefined biomarkers. Their recent ICML 2026 work, which uses self-supervised learning to capture neural activity across regions, channels, and time, supports broader efforts to bring intelligent neural interfaces closer to clinical applications, including through Infera Neuro , an EPFL spin-off co-founded by Shoaran. record.title: Show HN: Orisuji, a maze you solve by folding your phone
record.author: friggeri
record.story_text:
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo I felt the same excitement that I had felt when I got my first iPhone, way back when.

I remember playing Tap Tap Revenge, Fruit Ninja and all those other games that really took advantage of the new hardware to create new experiences. I also loved playing cute puzzles like Cut the Rope and Where’s my water.

A month ago, I got the itch to build something for the duo, in the lineage of those apps. Something that would be a fun puzzle with a unique game mechanic. I started with a simple premise: what if the cover screen was partly transparent? That could make a fun maze that you have to fold and unfold as you solve it.

Orisuji is a turn based paper maze, when the phone is open you have your base maze on the right part of the screen, but the only way to solve it is to figure out when to fold/unfold it to create bridges and new routes. Along the way you’ll encounter increasing complex levels: cats and foxes patrolling, doors you need to unlock, platforms you can toggle, and floors that crumble under you.

Some fun things I built/had to do that aren’t obvious:

- I built a web based level editor that runs the game’s rules engine compiled from Swift to wasm.

- Every level is validated by a solver that identifies shortest solutions, lints the board and identifies which “tricks” are required to solve it. This helped me a few times when designing levels where I would make a change but accidentally would introduce a shortcut.

- Figuring out how to translate the fold mechanic to non iPhone Duos was a cool challenge, I ended up adding a “virtual” on screen fold, which still doesn’t justice to the game.

- As much as I would love to have some data on how people play the game, it was super important to me that the game worked totally offline, not collecting any data.

It was so incredibly fun to build this, as you can expect I leaned heavily into agentic tools, which enabled me to move pretty fast. Every puzzled was however designed by hand, AIs are not good at “fun”, and from a game design perspective this was the most interesting part to me.

The whole game costs $4.99, all 69 levels (and already working on new worlds), no IAP ever.

Trailer: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w98lwzHgGWA

If you’ve got a duo (or not) I’d love to hear your feedback. And more than happy to answer anything about building/designing it!

Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key Learn to sing the songs you love. A free, open-source singing trainer for Mac that listens to the music you play. - dsmur

record.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
record.author: dsmurrell
record.story_text:
Hi all

I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.

Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.

So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!

It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.

So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.

It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.

During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).

You can check out a demo video on the site of me singing (warning given) here: https://singonkey.app

The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.

The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.

It’s still weak in a few places:

- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out

- sometimes it gets a note an octave off

- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point

- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on you

Would love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!
record.article_text: Learn to sing the songs you love. A free, open-source singing trainer for Mac that listens to the music you play. - dsmurrell/onkey Me singing along to a song OnKey learned from one play. The full demo, with sound . OnKey is a free, open-source singing trainer for the Mac. Play a song in Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube in a browser, and sing along. The first time, you get the lyrics, and OnKey learns the singer's melody when the song ends. After that, the notes scroll towards you, your pitch is drawn over them, and you get a score with a report on every line. OnKey doesn't provide, stream or download music. Your own music app plays it. You need a Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 or later) and macOS 14.2 or later. Download OnKey.dmg (from the latest release ), open it and drag OnKey to Applications. Setup asks for the microphone, to hear you, and for system audio recording, to hear the music app. It also asks whether OnKey may follow Spotify and Apple Music: choose Listen only and it follows songs by their sound alone. Getting started walks through it, and the FAQ answers the usual questions. When a song ends, OnKey learns it on your Mac: a model separates the lead vocal from the music, CREPE tracks the singer's pitch, and the GAME note model turns it into one bar per syllable. On later plays it finds its place from the music itself and tracks your voice live. Singing an octave down counts, and being a touch late isn't punished. How it works and Scoring have the details. OnKey never saves the music it listens to. It analyses the sound in memory as it plays. Your recordings and the songs it learns stay on your Mac (a take sung over speakers can contain some of the music). There's no account, no analytics and no crash reporting. Settings has a switch for Shazam, for lyrics and for the update check. Privacy lists everything OnKey keeps and sends, and scripts/release-hosts.txt lists every web address in a release. OnKey is for practising at home, with music you're entitled to play. Please: Rights holders can reach me at hello@singonkey.app ( LEGAL.md ). Use Report a problem in the app (Settings, the Help menu, or a take's page). It saves a zip of numbers and logs on your Mac, with no audio and no recordings of you, for you to attach to an issue if you want to. Troubleshooting covers the common problems. Questions, or a song that's out of step? Ask in OnKey's Discord , or email hello@singonkey.app . If you'd rather not trust my build, you can build your own. You need an Apple Silicon Mac with the Xcode command line tools, Rust, Node, and Python 3: Your build runs on your own Mac. The one thing it can't do is ask Shazam to name a new song, which needs my Apple signature. Spotify and Apple Music say what's playing themselves, so that only affects YouTube and Listen only. CONTRIBUTING.md has the details, the tests, and how to check a release's checksums. My releases are signed with my Apple Developer ID and notarised by Apple ( spctl -a -vv /Applications/OnKey.app shows who signed it). MIT. See LICENSE . Modified versions can't be called OnKey or use its icon. If you build on OnKey's code, a credit linking back here is appreciated. OnKey learns songs with CREPE, GAME, wav2vec 2.0 and UVR's MDX-Net Karaoke 2. The credits list each one, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md has the full notices and licence texts.

record.title: Flint homeowner questions sign stomping caught on video
record.description: A Flint homeowner is questioning why her political sign was knocked down after video showed a man walking onto her yard and stomping on it.
record.article_text: FLINT, Mich. — A Flint homeowner is questioning why her political sign was knocked down after video showed a man walking onto her yard and stomping on it. The video shows a man walking directly onto her front yard, knocking down the sign and walking away. Homeowner Kelsey Roke says she is disappointed by the incident. “Everyone has signs, posts, you know, all over their yard, whatever. And so, to me, it was just like, it was unnecessary, childish, and immature,” Roke said. “But yeah, it’s just disappointing, you know, to see that I live amongst people that are like this.” TV5 showed the video to Genesee County Prosecutor David Leyton, who said the conduct could be illegal. “So, you have a potential trespass, you have a potential malicious destruction of property, and if they take it away without the intent of returning it, then that’s a larceny,” Leyton said. During election season, Leyton says he sees situations like this one a lot. “Everybody has the right to their feelings in America. That’s the beauty of our country. But when I see something like that, you know, the next step is then some kind of a violent crime, politically motivated, and that’s just unacceptable,” Leyton said. As for Roke, she says no matter who you plan to vote for on Election Day, she hopes this incident encourages more people to show up at the polls. “Go out and vote regardless of what political party you’re affiliated with. You know, don’t let stuff like this that you see, uh, impact you to any degree,” Roke said. Roke said she has not decided whether to file a police report. Leyton said he encourages her to file one. record.article_text: Flint is distributing $1 million in opioid settlement funding to local organizations supporting youth services, financial stability and other community needs. FLINT, Mich. (WJRT) - The City of Flint is awarding $1 million in opioid settlement funding to local organizations working on programs aimed at supporting residents and neighborhoods. The city allocated the money to the Greater Flint Health Coalition, which oversaw the application and selection process. More than 40 organizations applied for funding, with 17 selected to receive awards ranging from $20,000 to $150,000. The funded initiatives focus on several community needs, including youth services, financial stability and programs aimed at strengthening individuals, families and neighborhoods. Greater Flint Health Coalition President and CEO Jim Ananich said the settlement money comes from circumstances communities would rather not have faced, but said it is important the funding now be used to help people affected by the opioid crisis. “Obviously, we wish the lawsuit never would’ve happened because then we wouldn’t have had these issues, but it did,” Ananich said. “And it’s important to make sure we put these dollars to good use, helping people that were affected so terribly in our community, across the state and across the country.” Ananich said the coalition wants to use the funding in ways that can support and expand work already happening in Flint. “We’re making sure that we’re using our dollars to leverage them to support people,” he said. Mayor Sheldon Neeley said the city plans to continue working with the Greater Flint Health Coalition and funded organizations after the awards are distributed. The city says recipients and their individual projects will be highlighted as the initiatives move forward.

text: From Toast to Bessemer: Who founders will hear from at TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 Building a startup means making decisions before you have all the answers. When should you scale? How do you know

record.title: From Toast to Bessemer: Who founders will hear from at TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026
record.body: Building a startup means making decisions before you have all the answers. When should you scale? How do you know you really have product-market fit? What does it take to land enterprise customers? How do you build the right team? And when you finally get in front of an investor, how do you make sure your pitch earns another conversation? On November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 will bring together founders, investors, and operators who have tackled those questions from different sides of the table. Hosted by TechCrunch in partnership with Fidelity Private Shares, the full-day event goes beyond fundraising and AI to explore the realities of finding customers, building teams, sharpening a pitch, developing founder leadership, and scaling companies both inside and outside traditional startup hubs. Save 25% on your ticket today , and bring a colleague along for free with our limited BOGO deal . Boston founders do not have to look far for an example of what can happen when a startup finds its market and continues evolving with its customers. Steve Fredette , president, co-founder, and director of Toast , takes the Impact Stage for “Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself.” Toast’s story offers founders a compelling case study in identifying a customer problem, finding product-market fit, winning customers, and ultimately scaling a Boston startup into a public company. But reaching scale does not mean the work is finished. Fredette’s conversation will look at what it takes to continue evolving a company as customer expectations, technology, and the market change around it, while staying connected to the needs that helped create the business in the first place. Kent Bennett , partner at Bessemer Venture Partners , will lead “Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale,” focusing on one of the most important questions an early-stage founder can answer: Are customers actually telling you that you are ready to grow? The session will give founders a chance to think more critically about the signals that matter before adding headcount, increasing spend, or accelerating go-to-market efforts. It is a useful counterpoint to startup culture’s constant pressure to move faster. Sometimes the smartest next move is making sure the foundation is actually there. That same tension takes center stage with Rudina Seseri , founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures . In “When to Scale and When to Hit the Brakes,” Seseri will explore how founders can distinguish between the moments that call for acceleration and the moments when restraint may protect the business. Founders are constantly making trade-offs between growth and discipline. Knowing when not to scale can be just as consequential as knowing when to go all in. AI is reshaping how new companies think about products, operations, and teams, but adding AI to an existing process is different from building a company around it from the start. Lior Div , CEO and co-founder of 7AI , will tackle that distinction in “Built for AI From Day One.” For founders building in the current technology environment, the conversation provides an opportunity to think beyond AI as a feature and toward how it can influence the architecture and operating model of an entire company. Chase Garbarino , CEO and co-founder of HqO , will take the Impact Stage for “The Boston Founder Playbook,” examining what it means to build and scale a company from Boston. For founders across New England and the broader East Coast ecosystem, the conversation offers a particularly relevant perspective on talent, customers, capital, and community outside the Bay Area. Combined with Fredette’s Toast story, it also gives this year’s Summit a strong local through line: Ambitious companies can be built in Boston, and founders here do not need to copy Silicon Valley to do it. A pitch does not have to close the deal. It has to make someone want the next conversation. Dave Balter , venture partner at True Ventures and CEO of Edisyl , will explore that idea in “Your Pitch Has to Earn the Next Conversation.” For founders accustomed to explaining their companies every day, the session is a reminder that knowing your business and communicating its story are two different skills. Later in the afternoon, attendees will see that theory put into practice. At “So You Think You Can Pitch?,” founders will put their stories to the test live on the Build Stage. Balter will be joined by Chirag Shah , partner at Define Ventures , and Simran Suri , principal at Maveron , as startups make their cases in front of an investor judging panel. For attendees, it is an opportunity to watch what happens when founders have limited time to make an idea connect, and to hear how investors react in real time. It is one of the most interactive parts of the Founder Summit program and a chance to learn from both the pitches that land and the ones that leave questions unanswered. The rest of the program stretches across many of the decisions founders are facing right now. Hunter Worland of NEA will explore why distribution may become a startup’s next competitive advantage. Vineet Edupuganti , co-founder and CEO of Cogent Security , will discuss building 10x teams. Tina Tosukhowong of TDK Ventures will examine the hidden signals that can identify category winners. Fidelity Private Shares will also bring its perspective to conversations about fundraising trends with Kristen Craft and enterprise relationships with Evan Schnidman . Together, the agenda creates a day that is not just about raising the next round or chasing the latest AI trend but is also about building the company. TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 takes place November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston. The day brings together candid founder conversations, practical sessions, smaller roundtables, live pitching, networking, and a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares. text: Blue Planet III is keeping the rough edges in the age of AI BBC’s Blue Planet III is keeping in shots that would normally end up on the cutting room floor to prove it’s real. BBC’s Blue Planet III is

record.title: Blue Planet III is keeping the rough edges in the age of AI
record.body: BBC’s Blue Planet III is keeping in shots that would normally end up on the cutting room floor to prove it’s real. BBC’s Blue Planet III is keeping in shots that would normally end up on the cutting room floor to prove it’s real. BBC’s Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots. Previous incarnations of the nature series were defined by their gorgeous, crystal-clear footage that seemed almost too good to be real. But one dead giveaway of AI is when things look too polished and seamless. To counter that, Blue Planet III goes warts and all. Executive Producer Elizabeth White told The Guardian in the past, “the amount of plankton and things” floating in the water would have caused them to cut a shot. Or “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’” Instead, this time they’re leaving it all in to show a more authentic, organic version of the oceans. The series features incredible displays of dolphins trapping fish by plugging holes with sea sponges, inter-species fish communication, and 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed. White says that real ocean creatures “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine.”
record.author: Terrence O’Brien

text: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say The David A

record.title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom
record.body: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say The David Attenborough -narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said. Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hit BBC series is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam. Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated. The executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”. She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’” But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage. For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.” Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”. That includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger. Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures. Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II, ‘iguana v snakes’ sequence. Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. One episode shows how warmer seas caused by the climate crisis are killing off sea anemone where clown fish live and how they try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White. Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts. White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.” Asked if the BBC’s £500m cost-cutting drive would affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series. Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1 November on BBC1 and iPlayer
